k639: Laprakë is one of the fastest gentrifying parts of Tirana. The trauma hospital, the American Hospital, the new regional bus terminal and the old airfield all sit here, and the driver everyone points to is the Tirana–Durrës–Rinas rail node. What we publish for it is the official band alone — 93,600 to 113,000 lek/m² — and that is deliberate. The market does not yet quote Laprakë separately; it prices the area inside the Dritan Hoxha corridor alongside Bond Tower, so any per-square-metre figure you see attributed specifically to Laprakë is an inference rather than a measurement. That gap is exactly what makes it early, and also what makes it harder to value.

k646: The Artificial Lake and the Grand Park around it are the largest green asset Tirana has, and the buildings facing them are priced accordingly: new builds ask €2,400–3,000/m² and resale €2,000–2,700/m² in 2026. A luxury tower here set the national record at €10,000/m², which says more about that one building than about the district. Buyers are the local elite and foreigners, and the flats change hands slowly and expensively rather than often. The catch is that a view premium does not always come back as rent — pay for the park if you intend to live with it, not to let it.

k657: Lungomare is Vlora's seafront promenade and the most expensive address in the city: €2,500–3,500/m², roughly double the €1,700–1,800 it asked in 2022. A three-year doubling on a strip that cannot be extended is most of the explanation — supply is fixed and the buyers are foreign — but it also means you are buying at the top of a fast move rather than into one. Before committing, compare what the same money buys at Uji i Ftohtë, which runs 20–25% below this strip, and check the completion status of anything sold off-plan on the promenade.

k663: Mali i Robit asks €950–1,200/m², which makes it the cheapest point on the beach strip running south from Durrës — below Golem and less than half of Qerret’s first line, on the same coast. The discount is not a mystery: it is further from the city, thinner on services, and it has none of the resort infrastructure that lets Gjiri i Lalzit or Qerret charge a premium. Worth being clear about the evidence, too — this figure comes from listing data alone. No agency survey or press series covers Mali i Robit separately, so treat it as a starting point for negotiation rather than a settled market rate.

k670: Myslym Shyri is a working shopping street rather than a showpiece, and that is the point: shops, schools and the centre are all within walking distance, which keeps local demand steady year after year. New builds ask €2,000–2,500/m² and resale €1,500–2,000/m²; a one-bedroom rents for €350–450 a month and a two-bedroom for €500–750. Flats here sell faster than in most of the city because the buyer pool is wide — families, professionals, and landlords who want tenants they will not have to replace every season. The street straddles two administrative units, so its official reference rate spans 114,300–192,800 lek/m² rather than sitting at one number.

k681: Orikum is the cheap end of the Vlora bay: €1,300–1,500/m², where the lower segment has moved up from €800/m² — a 63% rise — and the ceiling sits around €1,500. The marina redevelopment dominates local coverage of the town, but the existing stock still prices well below Lungomare, and it is that existing stock, not the renderings, that you are most likely buying. The state reference price is 61,400 lek/m², about €625, and notary and tax costs are calculated from that figure rather than from the market band above.

k687: Parrucë carries the busiest apartment market in Shkodra by volume, 228 listings on MerrJep in August 2026, and the lowest prices of the three researched quarters: resale at a median €870/m², new builds at €1,182/m², €909/m² across 23 listings. The 36% gap between new and old stock is the widest in the city, which is what a mixed-stock quarter looks like once a few new projects land in it. A 1+1 rents for €163–255 a month in the lek-denominated segment (31 listings), while furnished euro-priced units ask considerably more; against peripheral purchase prices that works out near 3.2–4.7% gross, before costs and vacancy. Parrucë reads as a yield-led buy rather than a lifestyle one. All figures are asking prices from listings.

k695: Paskuqan grew as the largest area of informal construction of the 1990s, and legalisation through ALUIZNI and the cadastre has moved slowly ever since. That history is what the price reflects: new builds around €1,200/m², up 14% year on year from €850–900 in 2023, with older stock at €600–1,100/m². Before anything else here, check the title and check what stage of legalisation the building is at — this is the one district in our coverage where that question decides whether the purchase is a bargain or a problem. Infrastructure and public services are still thin, and they are improving on municipal rather than market timelines.

k702: Pazari i Ri (the New Bazaar), renovated in 2016, is Tirana’s revived market quarter within the central Qendra area and one of the city’s best short-stay locations. Restaurants, cafés and the covered market draw steady tourist footfall, which supports strong holiday-rental demand. Housing here is part of the wider centre: older stock and new projects sit side by side, with 2026 prices broadly in line with the central market — from around €2,300/m² for new builds, higher near the square. The trade-offs are noise and tourist bustle; the appeal is character, walkability and rental potential.

k708: Plazh is the mass beach segment of Durrës: €1,200–1,700/m², up as much as 21% year on year from a €1,000–1,300 band. It is the strip most buyers mean when they say “an apartment by the sea in Durrës” — direct beach access, dense mid-rise stock, and a rental season that runs on domestic and diaspora demand rather than on foreign tourism. Because the stock is dense and much of it is alike, what moves price here is metres to the sand, not finish quality: compare the exact distance and the floor before you compare the price per square metre.

k715: Plepa reads as one zone and prices as two. Mass stock asks €1,000–1,270/m²; anything with a real sea view asks €1,800–2,160/m² — and a single headline range for the district (€1,000–2,160, across 159 listings in the second half of 2026) hides that split entirely. It is a quiet residential part of Durrës with established infrastructure rather than a resort strip. Work out which of the two segments a listing belongs to before you judge whether its price is fair: here you are paying for the view, not the address.

k720: Qendra — the centre around Skanderbeg Square — mixes older stock with new projects near the square. As of 2026, older apartments trade around €1,500–2,500/m² while new developments by the square reach €3,000–3,500/m²; inside the Small Ring, new builds start around €2,300/m². The centre offers unbeatable access to institutions, culture and transport, and strong short-stay demand. The trade-offs are noise, a mix of building ages and tourist bustle. It suits buyers who want a central, liquid address and accept a heterogeneous housing stock.

k725: Qerret sits past Golem on the same beach strip and has been the fastest-appreciating zone in the Durrës agglomeration, up 21–43% year on year. Prices step sharply with distance from the water: €1,100–1,500/m² behind the villas, €1,700–2,000 nearer the sea, and €2,200–2,500 on the first line, where almost nothing new is being built. Buyers are mostly Polish and Czech alongside the Albanian diaspora. One thing to know before you sign: Qerret is administratively Bashkia Kavajë, not Durrës, so permits, legalisation files and the enforcement cases documented in the area are handled by a different municipality than the city name suggests.
